title: Encryption, Encryption Protocols and Digital Certificates
overview: A2 security focuses on protecting communication and proving identity. You must compare symmetric/asymmetric encryption, understand public/private key use for confidentiality and digital signatures, explain certificates and TLS/SSL, and know the idea, strengths and limitations of quantum cryptography.
syllabusPoints: Explain plaintext, ciphertext, encryption/decryption and symmetric/asymmetric encryption.
Explain use of public/private keys for confidential messages and authentication/signatures.
Explain SSL/TLS and how certificates establish trust.
Explain digital signatures and digital certificates.
Explain the purpose, benefits and limitations of quantum cryptography.

definitions.definition: Encrypted data intended to be unreadable without the correct key.
The same secret key is used for encryption and decryption.
A related public/private key pair is used for complementary operations.
Cryptographic evidence that helps verify sender authenticity and detect alteration.
A digitally signed credential binding an identity to a public key.
A trusted organisation that verifies identity and signs digital certificates.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption
content: Fast and suitable for large amounts of data. The weakness is secure key distribution: both parties need the same secret key, and disclosure of it compromises confidentiality.

sections.title: Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality
content: To send a secret message to Bob, encrypt using Bob's PUBLIC key. Only the matching Bob PRIVATE key should be able to decrypt it. Public keys may be distributed openly; private keys must remain secret.

sections.title: Digital signatures
content: For authentication/integrity, the sender uses their private key in the signing process. A recipient verifies using the sender's public key. In real systems a hash of the message is normally signed, so modification can be detected efficiently.

sections.title: Certificates and trust
content: A certificate links a public key to an identified subject and is signed by a trusted CA. A client verifies the CA signature, validity dates and identity/hostname before trusting the key. This prevents an attacker from simply presenting an arbitrary public key as if it belonged to the genuine server.

sections.title: TLS/SSL
content: TLS (historically SSL) protects client-server sessions such as HTTPS. Certificates authenticate the server; asymmetric cryptography helps establish secure session secrets; efficient symmetric encryption then protects bulk traffic. The protocol also helps detect tampering.

sections.title: Quantum cryptography
content: Quantum key-distribution techniques can reveal eavesdropping because observation disturbs quantum states. Potential strength is secure key exchange based on physical principles. Limitations include specialised hardware, cost, distance/infrastructure constraints and the fact that compromised endpoints/software remain vulnerable.

examTips: Confidentiality: recipient public key. Signature/authentication: sender private key.
A certificate establishes trust in a public key; a signature verifies a message/sender—do not merge the two concepts.
Say what security property is achieved: confidentiality, integrity or authentication.
commonMistakes: Saying a public key must be secret.
Saying symmetric encryption uses a different key for decryption.
Saying TLS guarantees the endpoint itself contains no malware.
quickRecall: TLS uses asymmetric trust + symmetric session encryption
